blocks.text: OPINI - in many areas and countries with the majority of Christians, an inconspicuous irony is underway: in the midst of dominance of numbers, the Christian community is often pockets of poverty, scarcity, and loss of tenacity in forming civilizations.
The big question even comes up: can Christian faith and should be separated from social-political life?

An honest and historical answer is: no. Christianity from the beginning was a faith that grew to live in national cities. As Abraham Kuyper said, there's not an inch of our whole life where Christ doesn't say, "My God." In this view, faith in Christ covers the entire structure of social life, not just private spiritual space.

Unfortunately, post-illumination and secular liberalism spirit, many Christian theologies began to adopt a fake dichotomy between church and society, between sacred and secular. John Howard Yoder reminds you that the separation between church and politics is not a neutrality, but a church community. And that's what we're going through.
When the church lost its voice of prophecy and moral authority, it became an institution that depended on government grant or CSR corporation to survive.
Although Dietrich Bonhoeffer has warned us that the Church who is not willing to raise a vote for victims of injustice is no longer Christ's church, but is part of the world's system.

The Church should be a force of forming civilizations, not just the beneficiary of the system. In his history, the church created universities (like Oxford and Harvard), hospitals, operatives, and financial ethics systems that make up the modern world.
But today, churches in the pockets of Christians often become aid distribution agents, losing their culture mandate as a driving social transformation.

Therefore, it takes a reconstruction of a holistic Christian framework, not a fragmentalist. Miroslav Volf in A Public Faith (2011) confirmed: The unaffected faith in public space is a belief that doesn't touch reality. In other words, if Christianity wants to be relevant, it has to enter the political, economic and cultural structure without losing the integrity of the Bible.
The solution is not the political dominance of the church, but the strategic partnership between church, country and business in building civilization.
The Church brings ethics and spirituality, the state brings the structure of law and stability, business brings innovation and distribution of resources. All three could be partners, not enemies.
Christian regions today require the rise of prophecy and cultural vision united.

Without it, the Christian community will continue to be trapped in structural poverty and social helplessness. It's like being reminded by Lesslie Newbigin: the Church is a sign, a tool and the beginning of God's kingdom in the world.
It's time the church took that position again. Christian faith is not only for Sunday church, but for the world from Monday to Saturday.
